course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: Which group grew most as a result of industrialization?
choices: Serfs bound to the land
The hereditary nobility and the middle class of merchants and professionals
The industrial working class and the middle class
The hereditary nobility
questions.explanation: Factory workers and managers, professionals, and shopkeepers grew rapidly.
choiceExplanations: Factory workers and managers, professionals, and shopkeepers grew rapidly.
questions.distinguisher: The middle class grew, but the nobility's relative importance declined.

questions.prompt: The ideal of separate spheres held that
choices: men should earn wages and women should manage the home
women should work in factories and men at home
children should work for wages to support families
men and women should share all wage work and household work equally
questions.explanation: The ideal assigned paid work to men and the home to women.
choiceExplanations: The ideal assigned paid work to men and the home to women.
questions.distinguisher: Separate spheres divided roles by gender; it did not call for equal sharing.

questions.prompt: Cholera outbreaks in industrial cities were most directly caused by
choices: crowded housing and polluted water
the use of steam engines
the spread of labor unions
crowded housing and the use of telegraphs
questions.explanation: Contaminated water in crowded neighborhoods spread cholera.
choiceExplanations: Contaminated water in crowded neighborhoods spread cholera.
Steam engines did not cause cholera.
questions.distinguisher: Crowding mattered, but telegraphs have no connection to disease.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes a change in social hierarchy during industrialization?
choices: Social classes disappeared in industrial cities
Landholding nobles gained more status than at any earlier time
Wealth from business became a greater source of status
Birth became the only source of status
questions.explanation: Middle-class wealth gave new families influence.
choiceExplanations: Middle-class wealth gave new families influence.
questions.distinguisher: Business wealth rose in importance relative to landed nobility.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would best support the claim that separate spheres was mainly a middle-class ideal?
choices: Children attended school more often by 1900
Many working-class women worked in mills for wages
Middle-class magazines praised women's domestic role
Men worked in factories and mines
questions.explanation: Working-class women's wage labor shows they could not follow the ideal.
choiceExplanations: Schooling does not test the claim.
Working-class women's wage labor shows they could not follow the ideal.
This shows the ideal, not its limits.
Men's work does not test the claim.
questions.distinguisher: Magazines show the ideal existed, not that it was limited to one class.

governments should provide for every citizen
workers should form unions
individuals improve mainly through help from governments and charities
questions.explanation: He says self-help is the root of genuine growth.
choiceExplanations: He says self-help is the root of genuine growth.
questions.distinguisher: Smiles says help from without is often enfeebling.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Samuel Smiles, Scottish writer and reformer, Self-Help, first published in 1859
stimulusBlocks.citation: Samuel Smiles, Self-Help (London: John Murray, 1897), ch. 1. Project Gutenberg eBook #935.
stimulusBlocks.text: "HEAVEN helps those who help themselves" is a well-tried maxim, embodying in a small compass the results of vast human experience. The spirit of self-help is the root of all genuine growth in the individual; and, exhibited in the lives of many, it constitutes the true source of national vigour and strength. Help from without is often enfeebling in its effects, but help from within invariably invigorates. Whatever is done for men or classes, to a certain extent takes away the stimulus and necessity of doing for themselves; and where men are subjected to over-guidance and over-government, the inevitable tendency is to render them comparatively helpless.

questions.prompt: Smiles's ideas are best understood as reflecting the values of
choices: the landed nobility
Marxist socialists
the Tokugawa samurai
the industrial middle class
questions.explanation: Hard work, thrift, and self-improvement were middle-class ideals.
choiceExplanations: Hard work, thrift, and self-improvement were middle-class ideals.
questions.distinguisher: Marxists stressed collective action; Smiles stresses individual effort.

questions.prompt: Smiles's view differs most sharply from which of the following?
choices: Adam Smith's view of the division of labor in manufacturing
Marx and Engels's call for workers to unite
Adam Smith's support for free markets
middle-class praise of hard work
questions.explanation: Smiles stresses individual effort; Marx calls for collective revolution.
choiceExplanations: Smiles stresses individual effort; Marx calls for collective revolution.
Smith and Smiles both distrust government interference.
questions.distinguisher: Smiles's individualism fits with Smith, not against him.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, cholera spread in industrial cities because of
choices: the separation of spheres
polluted water in crowded neighborhoods
long factory hours
middle-class housing
questions.explanation: Polluted water in crowded areas spread cholera.
choiceExplanations: Polluted water in crowded areas spread cholera.
questions.distinguisher: Long hours harmed workers but did not spread cholera.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.9 key concept: new social classes, including the middle class and the industrial working class, developed, and family dynamics, gender roles, and demographics changed
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing social change in industrial cities, 1800–1900
stimulusBlocks.text:
Industrial cities grew faster than housing, water, and sewers. Working families crowded into tenements, and diseases such as cholera spread through polluted water. Factory work ran on the clock, often for twelve or more hours a day, and women and children worked in mills for lower pay than men.

A growing middle class of managers, professionals, and shopkeepers developed new ideals. Middle-class families often expected women to manage the home rather than work for wages, an ideal called separate spheres that few working-class families could afford to follow.

questions.prompt: The final sentence of the passage best supports which claim?
choices: All women stopped working for wages
Working-class families rejected the ideal because they preferred factory work
Middle-class women worked in mills
Separate spheres was an ideal many working families could not follow
questions.explanation: The passage says few working-class families could afford to follow it.
choiceExplanations: The passage says few working-class families could afford to follow it.
questions.distinguisher: The passage says they could not afford it, not that they rejected it.
